  handle is `io` with no host number, the family's rule.
  **Who may.** The host decides, and its refusal is **`denied`**
  (`EPERM`): the super-user may set any owner and group; anyone else
  may change the GROUP of a file they own to a group they are in, and
  may not give a file away. A change to the ids a file already has is
  one the host may still refuse to a process that does not own the
  file. **`invalid`** is also the host's own answer for an id it has
  no mapping for (a user namespace, `EINVAL`: measured, id 70000 in a
  container that maps `0..=65535`) and for a handle with no owner to
  change. **The host clears set-user-id and set-group-id** when an
  owner changes — linux and macOS both, the super-user's change
  included on a regular file (measured: `0o6755` reads `0o755` after)
  — so a program that wants those bits sets the owner FIRST and the
  mode after it (`fs_set_mode`), which is the order `cp -p` and
  `install` use. **Host posture:** `fchownat` and `fchown` on linux,
  macOS and freebsd; **windows has no owner or group of this kind and
  answers `unsupported`, by name**, after the shape. Every tier and
  both machines make the same one call, a path joined to the checked
  machine's own working directory first. **The cost, stated:** one
  system call; no stat before or after. Witnesses:
  `corpus/os/ids_rows.lu` (`invalid`, and the calls that change
  nothing, every host); on a host, `-1 -1`, the owner a file already
  has, `denied` for a user and the handle form; in a container as the
  super-user, an owner and a group set and read back, one left alone,
  a link itself against its target, a dangling link, the set-id bits,
  and as a user afterwards a group it is in against one it is not —
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/ids_lanes.rs`. (Written 2026-10-13, s236
  — wolf-lang#701.)

- `[os.fs.sync]` **The atomic save's syncs** (s248, wolf-lang#796;
  ruling #93; yew's G3). **`fs_sync(fd: int) -> () ! {io}`** puts the
  bytes and the metadata of the file behind a handle on the disk:
  `fsync(2)` on linux, `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)` on macOS (whose `fsync(2)`
  leaves them in the drive's cache) and `FlushFileBuffers` on windows,
  as Rust's `File::sync_all` makes each. 0..2 are the standard streams
  (`[os.fs.std]`). A closed or forged handle is `io` with no host
  number; every host refusal is `io` with its number in `os_error()`
  (`[os.fs.error]`): a pipe on linux and on macOS (measured), a windows
  handle open only for reading (access denied).
  **`fs_sync_dir(path: str) -> () ! {denied, invalid, io, not_found,
  unsupported}`** puts a directory's entries on the disk — the directory
  opened for reading (`O_DIRECTORY`, close-on-exec) and synced the same
  way — so that a creation, a rename or a removal in it survives a
  crash. A missing name is `not_found`, a name that is not a directory
  **`invalid`** (`ENOTDIR`), a refused search `denied`, anything else
  `io`. windows answers **`unsupported`** by name before the path is
  read: its directories are not opened as files, and NTFS orders a
  rename through its own log. **The atomic save** (yew's invariant 1)
  is five calls: create a temporary file in the target's directory
  EXCLUSIVELY, write it, `fs_sync` it, `fs_rename` it over the target
  (`rename(2)` replaces atomically on every unix host), and
  `fs_sync_dir` the directory. A crash between any two leaves the old
  file or the new one under the name, whole — never a mix and never
  neither: the first sync makes the new bytes durable before a name
  points at them, the second makes the name's move durable. **The
  exclusive create is the one wolf has** (ruling asked R3 in
  `[os.editor.calls.note]`, the recommendation implemented): open mode
  **4** (`[os.fs.open]`) and **`fs_open_perm(path, 4, perm)`**
  (`[os.fs.create.mode]`, the target's permission bits from the first
  instant) answer **`exists`** for a taken name on every machine,
  measured at 0.2.33 on the checked machine, native, release and lupin
  0.1.54 (s248's §2); no third spelling is added. Every machine makes
  the host's own calls (the checked machine through its own handle
  table and working directory). lupin 0.1.54 and 0.1.55 resolve neither
  name (wolf-interp#268). From 0.1.56, lupin serves both through
  `File::sync_all` (is79).
  **The cost, stated** (measured on the save's 24 bytes): linux on
  kasumi's btrfs, `fsync` 5–9 ms and the directory's 5–10 ms; macOS on
  CI's runner, `F_FULLFSYNC` 1–9 ms and the directory's 11 ms — the
  durable flush is the whole of it, one call each. Witnesses:
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/editor_calls_lanes.rs` —
  `fixtures/editor_calls/sync_rows.lu`, the rows on every machine (the
  pipe's row on unix), and `save.lu` under a fault shim
  (`faultshim.c`, `LD_PRELOAD` on linux, dyld interposing on macOS) that
  logs the storage calls on the save's own files and ends the program
  (`_exit`) before each in turn: whole, the log is the durable order —
  the temporary file opened exclusively, its writes, a sync of it
  (`fsync` on linux, `fullfsync` on macOS), the rename, a sync of the
  directory — and ended before any boundary the target holds the old
  bytes up to the rename and the new after it, never a mix: 11
  boundaries on the checked machine, 13 on each compiled tier (the
  runtime syncs a duplicate of the handle), on linux and macOS.

- `[os.fs.realpath]` **The canonical path** (s248, wolf-lang#797; yew's
  G4). **`fs_realpath(path: str) -> str ! {io, not_found}`** answers the
  absolute name `path` names with every symbolic link followed, every
  `.` and `..` taken — a `..` AFTER the link before it, so `l/..` is the
  parent of the link's target, not of `l` — and no trailing slash: what
  `realpath(3)` resolves (Rust's `fs::canonicalize`). A relative path is
  resolved against the working directory (the checked machine's own,
  `[os.fs.chdir]`). **`not_found`** is a missing name, a dangling link
  included, and the empty path; **`io`** is a loop of links, a component
  that is not a directory (on unix), a refused search, and an answer that is not
  UTF-8 (a `str` holds UTF-8; `fs_read_link` is the byte-exact call),
  with the host's number in `os_error()` where it gave one. macOS's
  `/tmp` answers `/private/tmp` (measured); windows answers the host's
  final name (Rust's `fs::canonicalize`: `GetFinalPathNameByHandleW`,
  the `\\?\` form it documents) and a name under a file `not_found`
  (measured). What it is for: an
  editor keys a workspace by its directory's canonical name, so two
  spellings of one directory are one workspace; a walk a component at a
  time with `fs_read_link` (boreutils' `paths.lu`) cannot take a `..`
  after a link, which needs the link's target. **The cost, stated:** one
  `realpath(3)` (a walk of the name with one `readlink` a link). lupin
  0.1.54 and 0.1.55 do not resolve it (wolf-interp#268). From 0.1.56,
  lupin canonicalizes inside its served tree and refuses an answer
  outside it by name (`[os.fs.path.domain]`), including this fixture's
  `/tmp` query. Witness:
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/editor_calls_lanes.rs`
  (`fixtures/editor_calls/realpath.lu`): a file, a directory with a
  trailing slash, a `..` after a directory and after a link, a dangling
  link and a missing name, a loop and a name under a file, on every
  machine.

- `[os.fs.access]` **May this process do it?** (s254, wolf-lang#820;
  yew yw02 G32). **`fs_access(path: str, mode: int) -> () ! {denied,
  invalid, io, not_found, unsupported}`** is `access(2)`: whether the
  process, by its **real** user and group ids, may do everything `mode`
  asks of what `path` names, a final link followed. `mode` is **0** (the
  name exists) or a sum of **4** read, **2** write and **1** execute —
  POSIX's `R_OK`, `W_OK` and `X_OK`, the same numbers on every unix host;
  outside `0..=7` it is **`invalid`**, decided before the host. Ok is a
  grant. **`denied`** is the host's refusal: `EACCES`, `EPERM` (linux: a
  write to an immutable file), `EROFS` (a write on a read-only mount — no
  write can succeed there, so it is a refusal and not an `io`) and
  `ETXTBSY`; **`not_found`** is a missing name, a dangling link included;
  everything else is **`io`** with the host's number in `os_error()` (a
  component that is no directory, a loop of links). Root is the host's
  rule: every read and write granted, an execute only where some execute
  bit is set. **The real ids, said:** they are the effective ones unless
  the program is set-id or has changed its ids (`[os.proc.ids.set]`); an
  open uses the effective ones, so such a program's answer can differ
  from what its open would do — `faccessat(AT_EACCESS)` asks that other
  question and is not added (ruling asked R1 in `[os.fs.gaps.note]`).
  **Advice, not a lock:** the answer can be stale by the next call; a
  program that must know opens, and the question exists to choose a path
  before any file is made (yew's save chooses between the atomic rename
  and the in-place write by whether the directory takes a write). The
  kernel's answer includes what a mode-bit test cannot see — an
  access-control list, a read-only mount — which is why yew's
  `directory_writable` (the mode bits against `os_euid`, `os_egid` and
  `os_groups`, before s254) was a workaround and not the call. **Host
  posture:** linux, macOS and freebsd ask `access(2)`; **windows answers
  `unsupported`** by name, after the mode's check, because its permission
  is an access-control list the three bits do not describe; **PAX**
  serves `access`, `faccessat` and `faccessat2` with the real ids (pax
  `kernel/files/files.lu`, px27), read from its source and not run here.
  The checked machine asks the host, the path against its own working
  directory (`[os.fs.chdir]`). `fs`. **The cost, stated:** one
  `access(2)`; nothing allocated. lupin 0.1.55 does not resolve it.
  Witness: `crates/wolf_driver/tests/fs_gaps_lanes.rs`
  (`fixtures/fs_gaps/access_rows.lu`: a file that exists, reads, writes
  and does not execute; a writable and a 0500 directory; a missing name,
  a dangling link, a name under a file; modes 8 and -1), on every
  machine; `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s crate tests. (Written 2026-10-21, s254 —
  wolf-lang#820.)

- `[os.fs.open.nofollow]` **An open that does not follow a final
  link** (s254, wolf-lang#820; yew yw02 G32). **Bit 16** of
  `fs_open_mode`'s and `fs_open_perm`'s mode is a flag, not a mode: added
  to any of `[os.fs.open]`'s six (`mode & 15` is the mode; any other bit
  above it is `invalid`, before the host, as every number outside the set
  always was), it carries `O_NOFOLLOW`, and a path whose LAST component is
  a symbolic link is refused — **`invalid`**, the host's `ELOOP`
  (freebsd's `EMLINK`) in `os_error()` — where the same open without the
  bit follows the link. A link in a middle component is followed either
  way: the bit names the last one only. A refused open creates and
  truncates nothing. Mode 4 (the exclusive create) answers **`exists`**
  on a link with or without the bit, as `O_EXCL` never follows one. A
  loop of links on the way is the host's same `ELOOP` and so the same
  `invalid` — one host number for both. **Why a bit and why `invalid`**
  (ruling asked R2): a bit serves both open calls and every mode with no
  new name, and answers no existing program differently (16 to 31 were
  `invalid` before); a released call's row set cannot grow (an exhaustive
  `match` over it would stop compiling), and `invalid` is that set's row
  for "this open, as asked, cannot be made of this argument" — `io` would
  hide the one answer a program acts on (the name is a link now: refuse
  the save) behind the family's catch-all. **What it is for:** an editor
  saving IN PLACE resolves a link before its decision table and then
  opens the target; between the two a link put in the target's place
  would redirect the write. sagitta opens with `O_NOFOLLOW` throughout
  its save and journal; the port refused a final link with an `fs_lstat`
  before the open, a window the bit closes. **Host posture:** linux,
  macOS and freebsd carry the flag; **windows refuses the bit `invalid`**
  by name, before the host — its symbolic links are reparse points an
  unprivileged program cannot make (`[os.fs.symlink]`), and opening one
  without following it is another call (`FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT`
  and a check of what was opened), named here and left to a lane of its
  own (R2); **PAX** serves `O_NOFOLLOW` (px27), read from its source and
  not run here. The checked machine carries the flag on the same
  `OpenOptions`. **The cost, stated:** zero — one more bit on the open
  the program makes. lupin 0.1.55 refuses the bit as a mode outside its
  set (`invalid`, measured at s254's prediction commit). Witness:
  `fs_gaps_lanes.rs` (`nofollow_rows.lu`: a file under the bit in four
  modes, a final link refused in three with the target intact, a middle
  link followed, mode 4 on a link, the bits above), on every machine;
  `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s `the_nofollow_bit_refuses_a_final_link`. (Written
  2026-10-21, s254 — wolf-lang#820.)

- `[os.fs.lock]` **The advisory lock** (s254, wolf-lang#820; yew yw02 G32,
  the journal's owner). **`fs_lock(fd: int, kind: int) -> () ! {busy,
  invalid, io, unsupported}`** takes an advisory lock on the file behind
  a handle — kind **1** shared, **2** exclusive; anything else
  **`invalid`**, before the handle is looked at — and **`fs_unlock(fd:
  int) -> () ! {io, unsupported}`** releases it. The lock is **tried
  once and never waited for**: a conflicting lock held through ANOTHER
  OPEN of the file is **`busy`**, with the host's `EWOULDBLOCK` in
  `os_error()` (windows: `ERROR_LOCK_VIOLATION`, 33). **The lock belongs
  to the open file** — BSD `flock(2)`'s rule, through Rust's
  `File::try_lock`, `try_lock_shared` and `unlock`: `flock(2)` on linux,
  macOS and freebsd, `LockFileEx` over the whole file on windows. So two
  opens of one file conflict even in one process; the handle's duplicates
  — a child's copy through `os_spawn_fds`, a forked child's
  (`[os.proc.fork]`) — share its lock; the lock lasts until `fs_unlock`
  or until the last of them is closed; and closing some OTHER handle of
  the same file releases nothing. Unlocking a handle that holds none is
  ok on every host (windows' `ERROR_NOT_LOCKED` is not a refusal here). A
  second `fs_lock` on a handle that already holds one is the host's:
  unix converts it, shared to exclusive or back, and not atomically (the
  old lock may be gone when the new one is `busy`); windows answers
  `busy`. A portable program unlocks first. A closed or forged handle is
  `io`; `ENOSYS` (a kernel without the call) and `EOPNOTSUPP` (a
  filesystem that keeps no locks) are **`unsupported`**, by name.
  **Advisory, and where it is not:** on unix a lock binds only the
  programs that ask for one; **on windows it is mandatory** for the
  locked range — another handle's read or write of the file fails while
  it is held. **Why `flock` and not `fcntl`'s record lock** (ruling asked
  R3): sagitta's journal takes `fcntl(F_SETLK)`, whose lock is the
  PROCESS's and is dropped when the process closes ANY descriptor of the
  file — a program that opens its journal a second time, to read it, and
  closes that handle loses the lock without a word — and whose two handles
  in one process never conflict, so no row inside one process could show
  it held. Open-file locks (`F_OFD_SETLK`) fix both and are linux's
  alone. **What `flock` does not do:** on linux an `flock` lock and an
  `fcntl` lock do not see each other (`flock(2)`), so a wolf program and a
  C program locking one file in the two styles do not exclude each other
  there (macOS not measured); NFS on linux emulates `flock` with `fcntl`
  locks. No waiting lock is added (R3): a wait in the kernel parks a
  worker where a kill cannot reach it; a program polls with its own
  deadline. **Host posture:** linux, macOS, freebsd and windows as above;
  **PAX answers `unsupported`**: its kernel has no `flock` yet and answers
  it `ENOSYS`, as every call outside its table (pax `kernel/user/user.lu`),
  read from its source and not run here — a note for the px lane. The
  checked machine takes the host's lock on its own handles. `fs`. **The
  cost, stated:** one `flock(2)` (one `LockFileEx`) a call; nothing
  allocated. lupin 0.1.55 resolves neither name. Witnesses:
  `fs_gaps_lanes.rs` (`lock_rows.lu`: three opens of one file, an
  exclusive lock against both kinds, shared beside shared, the release by
  a close, the shape; in a throwaway container on linux), on every
  machine; `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s `the_lock_is_the_open_files`. (Written
  2026-10-21, s254 — wolf-lang#820.)

- `[os.fs.fstat.record]` **The full stat on a handle** (s254,
  wolf-lang#820; yew yw02 G32; wolf-lang#536's other half).
  **`fs_fstat_record(fd: int) -> List[int] ! {io}`** answers
  `[os.fs.stat]`'s twenty-word record — the same words, kinds, units and
  `have` bits — from ONE metadata read on the handle (`fstat(2)`;
  `statx(2)` on linux), so a program learns the identity (`dev`, `ino`),
  link count, mode, owner and nanosecond times of the file it HOLDS, with
  no path walked between the open and the question: an editor's "is the
  file I opened still the one under that name" after a rename, `cat`'s
  "is my input my output", `pwd`'s "does `$PWD` name where I am". 0..2 are
  the standard streams (`[os.fs.std]`). A handle never names a link (an
  open follows it, or refuses it, `[os.fs.open.nofollow]`), so `kind` is
  never 3; a pipe's end is 4, a socket 5. Every refusal is **`io`** — a
  closed or forged handle, a word outside `int` — because on a handle
  there is no name to be missing or refused. **Why a call of its own**
  (ruling asked R4): `fs_fstat`'s first word answers 0..2 where the
  record's answers 0..7, so growing `fs_fstat` would split one word's
  meaning between two lengths of one call, and a server's handle stat per
  request (lobo's `serve_file`) would mint twenty words where it reads
  three; an `fs_identity(fd)` of two words would leave the rest of the
  record behind a path stat. **Host posture:** `[os.fs.stat]`'s table,
  word for word: linux, macOS and freebsd every word; **windows** its
  column (the kind, the size, `modified_ms` and the three times; mode,
  nlink, uid, gid, blocks, dev, ino, rdev and ctime refused with their
  `have` bits clear), and, as for `fs_fstat`, a handle that is no disk
  file is kind 2; **PAX** answers `fstat` and `statx` with its own device
  numbers (px36), read from its source and not run here. The checked
  machine reads the same metadata. `fs`. **The cost, stated:** one host
  call and one twenty-word list (160 bytes), `fs_stat`'s. lupin 0.1.55
  does not resolve it. Witness: `fs_gaps_lanes.rs`
  (`fstat_record_rows.lu`: the record against `fs_stat` of the path —
  kind, size, mode, nlink, identity, the nanosecond mtime, `have`; after
  a rename the handle's identity is the new name's; a directory 1, a
  pipe 4; a closed and a forged handle `io`), on every machine;
  `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s `the_handle_record_is_the_paths`. (Written
  2026-10-21, s254 — wolf-lang#820.)

- `[os.fs.mkfifo]` **Making a fifo** (s254, wolf-lang#820; yew yw02 G32,
  the serial test's FIFO). **`fs_mkfifo(path: str, perm: int) -> () !
  {denied, exists, invalid, io, not_found, unsupported}`** is
  `mkfifo(3)`: a fifo named `path`, its permission bits `perm` less the
  process's umask (`fs_open_perm`'s and `fs_create_dir_mode`'s rule);
  `perm` outside `0..=0o777` is **`invalid`**, before the host; a taken
  name (a dangling link included) is **`exists`**, a missing parent
  **`not_found`**, a refused write of the directory **`denied`**
  (`EACCES`); a file system or kernel that makes no fifo is
  **`unsupported`** — `EPERM` (`mknod(2)`: "the filesystem does not
  support the type of node requested"; a fifo asks no privilege, so
  nothing else can mean it), `ENOSYS` and `EOPNOTSUPP` — and anything
  else `io`. What it makes is `[os.fs.stat]`'s kind 4, and
  `[os.fs.open]`'s mode 5 is the open that does not park on it.
  **Host posture:** linux, macOS and freebsd; **windows answers
  `unsupported`** by name, before the path is read (its named pipes live
  in another namespace, `\\.\pipe\`, and are servers, not files);
  **PAX answers `unsupported`**: its kernel makes no fifo yet and refuses
  `mknodat` of one `EPERM`, as a file system that cannot (pax
  `kernel/user/user.lu`, px45; read from its source and not run here) —
  a note for the px lane. The checked machine makes the
  host's fifo. `fs`. **The cost, stated:** one `mknodat(2)`. lupin 0.1.55
  does not resolve it. Witness: `fs_gaps_lanes.rs` (`fifo_rows.lu`, in a
  throwaway container on linux: made, kind 4 and 0600, `exists`,
  `not_found`, `invalid`; then mode 5 on it with no writer — a handle at
  once, `fs_fstat` kind 2, the record kind 4, a read `eof` — and a
  writer's byte read back), on every machine; `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s
  `mkfifo_makes_a_fifo`. (Written 2026-10-21, s254 — wolf-lang#820.)

- `[os.fs.nonblock]` **A handle that does not park, and the write that
  says what it took** (s254, wolf-lang#818; yew yw02 G30).
  **`fs_set_nonblock(fd: int, on: bool) -> () ! {invalid, io,
  unsupported}`** sets (`on`) or clears `O_NONBLOCK` on the open file
  behind a handle (`fcntl(F_GETFL)`, `fcntl(F_SETFL)`). The flag is the
  open file's, so the handle's duplicates (a child's copy) see it too,
  and a pipe's two ends are two open files. **0, 1 and 2 are
  `invalid`**, by name: their open file is shared with whoever started
  the process, and a flag set there outlives the program (a shell's
  terminal left non-blocking). A closed or forged handle is `io`.
  **`fs_write_some(fd: int, bytes: List[byte]) -> int ! {busy, invalid,
  io}`** makes ONE write of `bytes` — all of them or a first part — and
  answers how many the host took: at least 1 for a non-empty list, 0 for
  an empty one (the handle still checked). On a non-blocking handle that
  can take nothing now it is **`busy`**, the host's `EAGAIN` in
  `os_error()`; on a blocking one it waits as `fs_write_chunk` does, for
  the first byte only. 0..2 are the standard streams, 1 and 2 after std's
  own buffer is flushed (`[os.fs.std]`'s order); `invalid` is a list of
  the wrong element width (an FFI caller's); a closed or forged handle is
  `io`; a write to a pipe whose reader has gone meets the host's
  `SIGPIPE` first (`[os.fs.std]`), and a program that ignores
  `BROKEN_PIPE` sees `io` (`EPIPE`). **The other calls keep their rows
  on a non-blocking handle:** `fs_write_chunk` writes what the host takes
  and answers `io` with `EAGAIN` in `os_error()` — how much it wrote is
  lost, which is why `fs_write_some` exists — and `fs_read` and
  `fs_read_chunk` answer `io` with `EAGAIN` where there is nothing to
  read; `os_signal_wait_fds` is the wait before either
  (`[os.signal.wait.write]`). **Why `busy`** (ruling asked R5): the mark
  is s247's payload-free "not now, and not the host's fault"
  (`[os.proc.fork]`), and `EAGAIN` is that answer — the same host number
  `fs_lock` answers for a conflicting lock (`flock`'s `EWOULDBLOCK` is
  linux's and macOS's `EAGAIN`); a new mark would be a second name for
  one number. **Why a new write:** `fs_write_chunk` writes all or answers
  a row, so on a non-blocking handle the count is the one thing a caller
  needs and the one thing it cannot say, and its row set cannot grow.
  **What it is for:** a clipboard writer that pipes to a tool (`xclip`,
  `wl-copy`, `pbcopy`) must not hang when the tool never reads: the write
  end non-blocking, `fs_write_some` until `busy`, then a write wait on the
  end under a deadline — sagitta's `clipboard.c` loop. yew's
  `clip-pipe-write-blocks` witness parked for ever at 0.2.34 (exit 124
  under `timeout 3`); written with these calls it takes 65536 bytes on
  linux, answers `busy`, waits out a 25 ms deadline and gives up.
  **Host posture:** linux, macOS and freebsd; **windows:
  `fs_set_nonblock` answers `unsupported`** by name (an anonymous pipe
  there has no flag a program can rely on), and `fs_write_some` is served
  (one `WriteFile`, never `busy`); **PAX** serves both (`fcntl` with
  `F_GETFL`/`F_SETFL` and `O_NONBLOCK`, px17; `write`), read from its
  source and not run here. The checked machine sets the flag on its own
  descriptors and writes once; 1 and 2 are its capture, which takes
  everything. `fs`. **The cost, stated:** `fs_set_nonblock` is two
  `fcntl(2)`s (one when the flag is already as asked); `fs_write_some`
  one `write(2)` with no copy of the list. lupin 0.1.55 resolves neither
  name. Witnesses: `fs_gaps_lanes.rs` (`nonblock_rows.lu`, `clip_write.lu`,
  in a throwaway container on linux: the capacity taken then `busy`, the
  25 ms write wait, the room a read makes, the end made blocking again, a
  reader gone, the shape), on every machine; `wolf_rt::fs_gaps`'s
  `a_non_blocking_pipe_answers_busy_when_full`. (Written 2026-10-21, s254
  — wolf-lang#818.)

- `[os.fs.gaps.note]` **Design note: the fs gaps an editor met**
  (s254; wolf-lang#820, #818, #834). yew's port of sagitta's save path,
  journal and clipboard (yw02, G30 and G32) met five absences in the fs
  family and one in the pipe, each worked around by name; s254 added
  seven calls, one open flag and one wait bit (`[os.fs.access]`,
  `[os.fs.open.nofollow]`, `[os.fs.lock]`, `[os.fs.fstat.record]`,
  `[os.fs.mkfifo]`, `[os.fs.nonblock]`, `[os.signal.wait.write]`), and
  moved `os_cwd`'s answer into the region it is asked in
  (`[mem.region.escape]`, pelt sh22). The spellings beyond the contract
  are rulings asked; each recommendation is what was built.
  - **R1, access's ids.** (A) `access(2)`, the real ids — the issue's
    call and sagitta's; (B) `faccessat(AT_EACCESS)`, the effective ids,
    what an open would use. They differ only in a set-id or id-changed
    program. **Recommend A.**
  - **R2, the no-follow open.** The spelling: (A) bit 16 of the mode,
    both open calls; (B) a call of its own. The final link's row: (A)
    `invalid`; (B) `io` with `ELOOP`; (C) a new mark (`link`). windows:
    (A) the bit refused `invalid` before the host; (B) served by
    `FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT` and a check of what was opened, which
    CI's runner cannot exercise (no unprivileged links). **Recommend A,
    A, A.**
  - **R3, the lock.** (A) `flock` semantics, the open file's, through
    std's `File::try_lock` family (`LockFileEx` on windows); (B)
    `fcntl(F_SETLK)`, sagitta's, the process's; (C) `F_OFD_SETLK` on
    linux and `flock` elsewhere. Waiting: (A) none, tried once; (B) a
    kind bit that waits in the kernel. **Recommend A, A.**
  - **R4, the handle's identity.** (A) `fs_fstat_record`, the path
    record's twenty words; (B) `fs_fstat` grown to twenty; (C)
    `fs_identity(fd) -> (int, int)`. **Recommend A.**
  - **R5, `EAGAIN` and the write.** The row: (A) `busy`, with the lock's
    conflict (one host number); (B) a new mark (`again`). The write: (A)
    `fs_write_some`, one write and its count; (B) `fs_write_chunk` on a
    non-blocking handle (no count to answer, no row to add). **Recommend
    A, A.**
  - **R6, write readiness.** (A) bit 62 of an element of
    `os_signal_wait_fds`'s list (no new name; no program answered
    differently); (B) a second list, `os_signal_wait_fds_rw(r, w, set,
    deadline)`; (C) a parallel list of interests. **Recommend A.**
  - **R7, the standard streams and the flag.** (A) `invalid` by name; (B)
    served. **Recommend A.**
  - **R8, capabilities.** All seven calls are `fs`, with the family.
    **Recommend as listed.**
  **PAX** (read from pax trunk `241b3229`'s source, not run): access,
  `O_NOFOLLOW`, `fcntl(F_SETFL)` with `O_NONBLOCK`, `poll`'s `POLLOUT` and
  `fstat`/`statx` are served; `flock` answers `ENOSYS` (no such call in
  its table) and `mknodat` of a fifo `EPERM` (refused by name), which the
  runtime answers `unsupported` by name — the two absences, for the px
  lane. **lupin** 0.1.55 resolves none of the seven names and refuses
  the open's bit as a mode outside its set; wolf-interp owes each (resolve
  and serve inside its tree, or refuse by name: it admits no `unsafe`, and
  `access(2)`, `mkfifo(3)` and `fcntl(2)` are not in Rust's standard
  library; `File::try_lock` is) and `os_cwd`'s place in the region.

- `[os.fs.change.note]` **Design note: the calls that change a file**
  (s230; wolf-lang#346, #698, #699, #700, #702, #704). s218 let a
  program read what `ls -l` shows; these seven calls and the mask let
  it write the same words, which is what `chmod`, `touch`, `ln`,
  `mkdir -m`, `cp -p` and a shell's `umask` are. **One order for every
  call:** the SHAPE of the arguments first (`invalid`, the same on
  every host), then the HOST (`unsupported`, by name, where it has no
  such operation), then the host's one call and its own error through
  the family's mapping — `os_exec`'s order (`[os.proc.exec]`), so a
  malformed call is `invalid` on windows too. **Per host:**

  | call | linux, macOS, freebsd | windows |
  |---|---|---|
  | `fs_set_mode` | `chmod` | `unsupported` |
  | `fs_open_perm`, `fs_create_dir_mode` | `open`, `mkdir` with the mode | `unsupported` |
  | `fs_symlink` | `symlink` | `unsupported` |
  | `fs_link` | `linkat`, no flag | `CreateHardLinkW` |
  | `fs_set_times` | `utimensat` | the two times on an attribute handle |
  | `fs_truncate` | `ftruncate` | `SetEndOfFile` |
  | `os_umask` | `umask` | `unsupported` |

  **Every machine.** native and release make the call through
  `wolf_rt`; the checked machine makes the same call, a path joined to
  its own working directory first (`[os.fs.chdir]`); the freestanding
  target refuses each by its name (`[abi.target.none]`). lupin, which
  forbids `unsafe` and links no libc, serves what the Rust standard
  library reaches — the mode, both creations, both links, the length,
  and the times of a path it can open, following a link, with "now"
  read from its own clock — and refuses by name what the library does
  not: `os_umask` whole, and `fs_set_times` on a link itself. None of
  the eight allocates: each answers `()` or one `int`, so no region
  rule reads them.
  **What was not done**, each left to its issue: owner changes
  (wolf-lang#701; since done by s236, `[os.fs.owner]`), holes and
  reflinks (#703), fifos and device nodes
  (#705), a rename that does not replace (#706), calls relative to an
  open directory (#707), a path that is not UTF-8 (#687), and the
  handle forms of the mode and the times (`fchmod`, `futimens`), which
  nothing has yet needed.
  **The spellings and shapes were ruled on 2026-10-11 (ruling #67):
  each as recommended below, which is what is implemented. The
  options are kept as the record of what was weighed:**
  - **R1, the mode change.** (A) `fs_set_mode(path, mode)`, following a
    final link — the fs family spells its operations out
    (`fs_read_link`, `fs_create_dir`), the record calls the word
    `mode`, and it pairs with `fs_set_times`; (B) `fs_chmod`, POSIX's
    name, as `os_chdir` and `os_umask` are — but those are the `os_`
    family's habit; (C) a `follow` argument, as `fs_set_times` has —
    linux has no call that changes a link's mode, so false would be
    `unsupported` on the commonest host; (D) the handle form instead
    (`fchmod`) — closes the race between a creation and its mode, which
    R2 closes at the creation. **Ruled A.**
  - **R2, a mode at creation.** (A) two new calls, `fs_open_perm(path,
    open, mode)` and `fs_create_dir_mode(path, mode)`, the bits
    `0..=0o777` less the umask; (B) a mode argument added to
    `fs_open_mode` and `fs_create_dir` — every existing call site
    changes arity for a word most never want; (C) the umask alone — set
    it around the creation: process-wide, so it races every other task;
    (D) wolf-lang#346's first sketch, `fs_create_mode(path, bits)`,
    exclusive creation only — `cp` creates or truncates. **Ruled
    A.**
  - **R3, the links.** (A) `fs_symlink(target, path)` and
    `fs_link(existing, path)`, in `ln`'s and the system calls' order,
    the target verbatim, an empty target `invalid`, `fs_link` never
    following `existing`; (B) a `follow` argument on `fs_link`
    (`ln -L`) — one more word on every call for the rare one, and
    `fs_read_link` already lets a program resolve first; (C) the
    target as `List[byte]`, as `fs_read_link` answers it — right for a
    name that is not UTF-8, and that is the byte-path lane's (#687),
    for every path at once. **Ruled A.**
  - **R4, the times.** (A) one call, the two times as seconds and
    nanoseconds, the special values in the nanosecond word (`-1` now,
    `-2` leave) where POSIX keeps them, and `follow`; (B) a flags word
    beside four plain numbers — a second place for the same two bits;
    (C) separate `fs_set_atime`, `fs_set_mtime` and `fs_touch` — three
    names, and "set both to different times at once" becomes two calls
    with the first one's change visible in between; (D) milliseconds,
    as `fs_modified_ms` reads — it cannot write back what `fs_stat`
    read. **Ruled A.**
  - **R5, the length.** (A) `fs_truncate(fd, len)` on a handle,
    `invalid` for a negative length and `io` for every host refusal;
    (B) the path form — one more open inside the runtime, and no way
    to truncate the file a program is writing; (C) both. **Ruled
    A.**
  - **R6, the mask.** (A) `os_umask(mask) -> int`, set-and-answer, the
    two-call read stated with its caveat; (B) also a read that changes
    nothing — linux can answer one from `/proc/self/status`, macOS and
    freebsd have no such call, so it would be `unsupported` on two
    tier-1 hosts or a set-and-restore in disguise; (C) `os_umask(-1)`
    as the read — the same disguise, with a magic number. **Ruled
    A.**
  - **R7, windows.** (A) `unsupported` by name for the mode, the moded
    creations, the symbolic link and the mask, and the hard link, the
    times and the length served; (B) `fs_set_mode` mapped onto the
    read-only attribute — success reported for a mode that was not
    set; (C) `fs_symlink` attempted, `denied` without the privilege —
    a call whose answer depends on a machine setting, and which must
    guess the link's kind. **Ruled A**, as `[os.fs.stat]` answers
    no mode there and `[os.proc.exec]` no exec.
  - **R8, capabilities (ruling #54's reasoning).** The seven `fs_*`
    calls are `fs`. `os_umask` is `env`: it changes process state every
    later creation reads, as `os_chdir` changes the directory every
    later path reads. **Ruled as listed.**
  - **R9, the checked machine's mask.** (A) the process's own, really
    set, with the embedding caveat `[os.fs.umask]` states; (B) a
    machine-local mask applied by swapping the real one around each
    creation under a lock — other threads' creations see the swapped
    mask for the length of a system call; (C) a machine-local mask
    repaired by a `chmod` after each creation — the window the mask
    exists to close. **Ruled A.**
  - **R10, lupin.** (A) what the Rust standard library reaches, the
    rest refused by name (`os_umask`; a link's own times); (B) a safe
    system-call crate, which would serve both exactly — ruling #57's R8
    asked the same question of the terminal calls and answered A.
    **Ruled A**; B stays the question ruling #57's R8 left, and
    these two calls are now part of what it would buy.

## §7 The host builtin table `[os.host]`

(Written 2026-09-15, s163 — wolf-lang#181. `[gram.expr.tagident]`
makes a bare identifier in a handler a tag "exactly as wide as the
declared row", and for a module callee that row is in its signature;
for a builtin — `net_connect`, `os_wait`, `env_get`, `json_get` — no
pinned document declared one, and each machine carried an
implementation-local table probed off the other's behaviour.)

- `[os.env.argv]` **The invocation name and byte arguments.**
  `env_arg0()` answers argv[0] exactly as invoked, not the resolved
  executable (`os_exe`). `env_args()` answers argv[1..] in order.
  Both return text without lossy decoding: if an argument they read is
  not UTF-8, the outcome is `trap(argument-utf8)`, exit 134 at the
  native process boundary, with the message
  `argument N is not UTF-8; read it with env_args_bytes()` where N is
  the OS argv index (the name is zero). `env_args()` does not decode
  argv[0]; `env_arg0()` does not decode the remaining arguments.
  `env_args_bytes()` answers every argument, **argv[0] first**, as
  `List[List[byte]]`, with no decoding, omitted entry, or terminating
  NUL. Unix argument bytes are verbatim; Windows uses WTF-8 for the
  OS's UTF-16 arguments (the OS-string encoding of
  `fs_read_dir_entries`). An absent argv[0] makes `env_arg0()` empty
  text and an absent argv makes both list readers empty.
  `env_get` still answers its `utf8` row; `env_vars` still omits
  non-UTF-8 entries. Neither uses the text argv reader.
  The name and byte-list answers are materialized in the ambient
  region; `env_arg0` is a `[mem.region.escape]` site, as `os_cwd` is.
  These are hosted-runtime calls: the freestanding target refuses
  `env_arg0` and `env_args_bytes` by name, as it refuses `env_args`.

- `[os.host.sigs]` **Every host builtin's signature, its row included,
  is the table below**, and a builtin call's declared row — the row
  `[gram.expr.tagident]` reads, the row a `match` over a caught value
  is exhaustive against, the row `?` propagates — is its row here and
  nothing wider or narrower. A line reads `name(parameter types) ->
  result`; a fallible result is `T ! {tags}`, the tags written in
  sorted order because a row is a set (`[gram.type.row.flatten]`), and
  no tag carries a payload (D30's payload-less v0 rows). A builtin the
  table does not list has no row: the output and sync surface (`print`,
  `print_raw`, `eprint`, `eprint_raw`, `List`, `Map`, `Pool`, `Mutex`,
  `channel`, `range`), the helpers `min` and `zip`, the comptime
  intrinsics (`reflect`, `typeinfo`, `typebuild`, `implements`,
  `size_of`) and `assert` are typed by their own clauses, and
  `acquire`, `release`, `build_config`, `build_batch`, `worker` and
  `sleeper` are the s02 corpus stand-ins, not language. WHICH tag a
  failing call raises is each call's own clause (`[os.fs.open]`,
  `[os.fs.remove]`, `[os.net.accept]`, …); this table fixes only the
  set. **The table is the compiler's, byte for byte**: `wolf_sema`'s
  `host_builtin_sig` renders these lines, and the crate test
  `tests/host_table_spec.rs` reds when a signature and this block part
  in either direction, so a builtin cannot gain, lose or retag a row
  without this clause moving in the same commit. **The cost, stated:**
  none — a table is a static fact; a row is checked where the call is
  typed and adds nothing to the call.
  **The interpreter against it** (lupin 0.1.36, measured by s163 on
  linux: each fallible builtin called with an argument that fails
  harmlessly, under a handler naming exactly this table's tags, so a
  tag missing from lupin's own row would fall to an earlier arm as a
  binder; 56 of the table's 57 fallible builtins, `os_signal_wait`
  left out because it parks). 45 of the 56 calls agree in verdict and
  stdout with wolf's native tier, 34 of them raising a tag the table
  lists; lupin raised no tag outside it. Eight part by scope — lupin does not resolve
  `fs_create_dir`, `fs_remove_dir`, `fs_write_chunk`,
  `net_writev_head`, `os_signal_listen`, `os_signal_raise` or
  `read_line`, and refuses `net_adopt_listener` by name — and three

  `fs_rename` of a missing file raises `cross_device` there and
  `not_found` here, and `net_read`/`net_read_bytes` of a forged handle

  checks no row (a handler missing a tag passes its `resolve`), so the

## §8 The terminal `[os.term]`

(Written 2026-10-08, s219 — wolf-lang#622, pelt's H3.)

- `[os.term]` **The controlling terminal's foreground group and mode.**
  A session has one controlling terminal; one process group at a time
  is its **foreground** group — the group the terminal's interrupt,
  quit and suspend characters signal, and the only group that may read
  it — and the terminal has a **mode** (XBD 11). The calls take a
  handle as the fs family does (0..2 the standard streams, 3 and up a
  table handle such as `/dev/tty` opened with `fs_open_mode`) and act on
  the terminal it names. A handle that is closed, forged or not a
  terminal is `io`; every call is `unsupported` on windows, whose
  console has no process groups.
  - **`os_pgid() -> int ! {unsupported}`** — this process's group id.
  - **`os_term_foreground(fd: int) -> int ! {io, unsupported}`** — the
    terminal's foreground group (`tcgetpgrp`).
  - **`os_term_set_foreground(fd: int, pgid: int) -> () ! {io,
    unsupported}`** — make `pgid` the foreground group (`tcsetpgrp`); a
    group not in this session, or not positive, is `io`. A process
    outside the foreground group that does this is sent `SIGTTOU`
    (default: stop) unless it blocks or ignores it, and a shell taking
    the terminal back from a finished job is exactly that process, so
    the call blocks `SIGTTOU` on the calling thread for its duration
    and restores the mask after; nothing else's mask moves.

- `[os.term.group]` **This process into a group** (s241,
  wolf-lang#762; ruling #79 R2). **`os_set_pgid(pgid: int) -> () !
  {denied, invalid, io, unsupported}`** moves the **calling process**
  into process group `pgid` — `setpgid(2)` with pid 0 — or, for a
  `pgid` of 0, makes it lead a new group whose id is its own process id
  (`os_pgid() == os_pid()` after). It acts on the caller only: a
  child's group is set at its spawn (`os_spawn_job`'s `group`,
  `[os.proc.job]`), never after, which is the race `[os.term.note]` R4(C)
  rejected. What it is for, measured (s240): an interactive shell leads
  a group of its own at start (`os_set_pgid(0)`) and goes back into the
  group it was started in at exit; GNU `timeout` leads a group before it
  runs its command so that `os_signal_send_group(os_pgid()?, m)` reaches
  everything the command started. The order of refusal: (1) the SHAPE
  — **`invalid`** for a `pgid` below 0 or past a process id's width,
  before the host; (2) the HOST — **`unsupported`** on windows; (3) the
  host's answer — **`denied`** (`EPERM`) for a session leader, which may
  not move, and for a group that is in another session or does not
  exist (both hosts, measured); **`invalid`** for `EINVAL`; **`io`**
  otherwise. `exec`, as the sends are (ruling #79 R6). On the checked
  machine it moves the `wolf` process, the process the program runs as
  (`[os.signal.checked]`).

- `[os.term.mode]` **The mode is one int.** **`os_term_mode(fd: int) ->
  int ! {io, unsupported}`** reads it and **`os_term_set_mode(fd: int,
  mode: int) -> () ! {invalid, io, unsupported}`** sets it: bit 0
  `CANONICAL` (1, input a line at a time with the terminal's own
  editing; `ICANON`), bit 1 `ECHO` (2; `ECHO`), bit 2 `SIGNALS` (4, the
  interrupt, quit and suspend characters raise signals; `ISIG`), bit 3
  `FLOW` (8, the start and stop characters resume and pause output and
  never reach the program; `IXON`, s234), bit 4 `EXTENDED` (16, the
  host's extended input processing — literal next, word erase, reprint,
  discard; `IEXTEN`, s234), bit 5 `RAW_CR` (32, a typed carriage return
  reaches the program as CR: `ICRNL` CLEARED; s248), bit 6 `RAW_OUTPUT`
  (64, bytes written reach the terminal as written, a LF a LF and not CR
  LF: `OPOST` CLEARED; s248), bit 7 `STRIP8` (128, input stripped to seven
  bits: `ISTRIP` set; s248), `VMIN` in bits 8..15 and `VTIME` (tenths of
  a second) in bits 16..23 — how a read waits when `CANONICAL` is off.
  Every other field of the terminal's settings is left as it is found,
  so a mode read and later set again restores exactly what was changed.
  **s234's one change of meaning:** before it a mode had no `FLOW` or
  `EXTENDED` bit and a set left `IXON` and `IEXTEN` as found; now a mode
  built by hand that omits them turns both off — a program that reads
  the mode and changes only the bits it means to is
  unaffected. **s248's three bits** (wolf-lang#802; yew yw01's W1,
  ruling asked R7 in `[os.editor.calls.note]`, the recommendation
  implemented) each name the setting a terminal does NOT usually have,
  so a 0 in each is what a terminal is given (`ICRNL` on, `OPOST` on,
  `ISTRIP` off): on such a terminal every mode a program read before
  them reads the same int, and every mode built by hand or by a std that
  predates them (wolf-std's `pack` at `cceda63` keeps bits 0..4) sets
  what it set. On a terminal whose settings differ from the usual ones
  (`stty -icrnl`, `-opost`, `istrip`), such a mode now writes the usual
  setting back where it left the flag as found before s248. What an
  editor's raw mode is, as C yew's sets it (`cfmakeraw`'s set): canonical,
  echo, signals, flow and extended off, `RAW_CR` and `RAW_OUTPUT` on —
  a typed Enter then reads CR (13), not LF (10, Ctrl-J's byte), and a
  written LF reaches the wire alone (measured by yw01 under a
  pseudo-terminal at 0.2.33, where neither was reachable). The other
  flags of that set — `INLCR`, `IGNCR`, `BRKINT`, `IGNBRK`, `PARMRK`,
  `INPCK`, `ECHONL`, the character size and parity — are left as found:
  the first two are off on every terminal a program is given, and the
  rest act on a serial line's breaks and parity, which a
  pseudo-terminal has none of. windows answers `unsupported` for the
  three as for every `[os.term]` call, after the shape. With `EXTENDED` on, macOS keeps Ctrl-V and Ctrl-O from the
  program even with `CANONICAL` off, where linux passes them (measured,
  sh11's `lnext_probe`); with `FLOW` on, Ctrl-S and Ctrl-Q never arrive.
  Any other bit (bit 24 and above, since s248), or a negative mode, is
  `invalid` before the handle is read. The set waits
  for output already written to drain and keeps input already typed
  (`TCSADRAIN`), and blocks `SIGTTOU` as `os_term_set_foreground`
  does. The runtime restores nothing on exit unless the program asked:
  a program that changes the mode restores it (std's `term` module pairs
  the two), or registers the restore with the runtime
  (`[os.term.restore]`, s248), which then restores it on every exit the
  runtime owns, a trap's and the stack guard's included.

- `[os.term.restore]` **The terminal restored at every exit the runtime
  owns** (s248, wolf-lang#794; ruling #93 R1 C; yew's G1).
  **`os_term_restore_at_exit(fd: int, mode: int, bytes: List[byte]) ->
  () ! {invalid, io, unsupported}`** registers, for this process, a
  restore of the terminal `fd` names: when the process ends by an exit
  the runtime owns, the runtime sets that terminal's mode to `mode` —
  exactly as `os_term_set_mode(fd, mode)` sets it (`[os.term.mode]`:
  `TCSADRAIN`, `SIGTTOU` blocked) — and then writes `bytes` to it (an
  editor's alternate-screen leave and cursor show, say). **The exits it
  owns:** a return from `main` (the entry shim restores before it
  returns, in a program that names the call — every other program's
  shim is unchanged), `os_exit`, an error returned from `main` (D30's
  exit 1), a trap — after the `wolf-trap:` report, before the process
  ends (134) — the stack guard's overflow report, `os_exit_signal`
  before its raise (`[os.signal.exit]`), and the death of the proc
  root (`[conc.proc.root]`). The restore runs **in the runtime, never in
  a handler of the program's** (`[os.signal.model]` stands): the trap
  path already ran runtime code before it ended the process, and the
  guard's report is the runtime's own async-signal-safe code, where the
  restore uses only `tcgetattr`, `pthread_sigmask`, `tcsetattr` and
  `write`, allocates nothing and claims the registration with one atomic
  try. **One registration a process; the last call wins** — its
  duplicate of the descriptor replaces the one before, which is closed;
  each restore takes the registration, so it runs once. A registration
  of the mode the terminal already has is allowed (a program may
  register first and change the mode after, or the other way round).
  The runtime holds a **duplicate** of the terminal's descriptor from
  the call (at 3 or above and close-on-exec, never one of the standard
  three, s245's rule), so a handle the program closes before it ends
  still restores; the bytes are copied at the call. **What it does not
  cover, said here:** a death by a signal the program never listened for
  — `KILL`, a `TERM` or `HUP` under its default disposition, a fault
  outside the stack guard — runs no code of the process, the runtime's
  included, so nothing is restored; C yew's own guarantee holds only
  where a handler runs, and a wolf program listens for `TERMINATE`,
  `RELOAD` and `QUIT` (`[os.signal.listen]`) and ends through `os_exit`
  or `os_exit_signal`, which restore. An `os_exec` replaces the image:
  the registration ends with it and nothing is restored
  (`[os.proc.exec]`). A child that a fork makes is another process and
  restores nothing (the registering pid is kept and compared). **The
  order of refusal:** a `mode` outside `[os.term.mode]`'s bits is
  **`invalid`** before the handle is read; then windows is
  **`unsupported`**, by name, as for every `[os.term]` call; then a
  handle that is closed, forged or not a terminal is **`io`**, and so is
  a duplicate the host will not make (ruling asked R1 in
  `[os.editor.calls.note]`, the recommendation implemented: the
  contract's `{invalid, unsupported}` left the family's `io` row out).
  `io`, with `os_term_set_mode`, at comptime and in a manifest (ruling
  asked R5). **The checked machine** restores on its own exit path: it
  holds the registration (a duplicate of the host's terminal descriptor)
  and restores when its run ends, whatever the verdict — an exit, a
  trap, an error from `main`, or an `unsupported` end (its call-depth
  budget, where a compiled tier's stack guard reports; and
  `os_exit_signal`, which it refuses by name) — so `conform-run
  --checked` leaves the terminal as a compiled program does. lupin 0.1.54
  and 0.1.55 do not resolve the call (it links no libc, so it owes the
  shape rows and a refusal by name, wolf-interp#268). **The cost, stated:** one descriptor and the
  bytes, held from the call, only in a program that makes it; one call
  before `main`'s return in a program that names it; nothing on any
  other program's exit (a null check of the registration at the
  runtime's exits). Witnesses: `crates/wolf_driver/tests/
  editor_restore_lanes.rs` — yw00's shape (`notes/yw00-evidence/
  witness/trap-leaves-raw.lu`: raw mode, then a bounds trap) and every
  other exit, each on a pseudo-terminal `script(1)` makes in a throwaway
  container (linux) or the test opens on CI's macOS runner: the
  terminal's settings after equal those before (on macOS less `PENDIN`,
  the kernel's "retype pending input" state flag, which it sets when
  input goes back to canonical, as after any `stty icanon` — measured,
  run 39338977636), and the bytes follow the program's last line; the two limits (no registration; a `TERM`
  sent to itself under the default) leave it raw; the last
  registration's bytes alone; the mode the terminal already has — on
  the checked machine and both compiled tiers, the binaries also under
  `taskset -c 0-3` on linux; the rows on every host,
  `editor_calls_lanes.rs` (`restore_rows.lu`).

- `[os.term.size]` **The window's size** (s234, wolf-lang#719).
  **`os_term_size(fd: int) -> (int, int) ! {io, unsupported}`** answers
  the rows and the columns of the terminal `fd` names, as the terminal
  holds them (`TIOCGWINSZ`, `ioctl_tty(2)`): what the emulator last
  told it, or what `stty rows … cols …` set. A size the terminal was
  never told is 0 (a pseudo-terminal nobody sized), and a program falls
  back on `COLUMNS` (XBD 8.3) or 80 as it would without the call. When
  the window changes the foreground group is sent `SIGWINCH` — the
  meaning `RESIZE` (`[os.signal.set]`, s232's bit 16384; #719 asked for
  bit 512, written before s232 gave 512 to `USER`) — and the next call
  answers the new size. A handle that is closed, forged or not a
  terminal is `io`; windows is `unsupported`, as for every `[os.term]`
  call.

- `[os.term.chars]` **The special characters** (s234, wolf-lang#719).
  **`os_term_chars(fd: int) -> List[int] ! {io, unsupported}`** answers
  twelve characters of the terminal's settings, always in this order:
  0 erase (`VERASE`), 1 kill (`VKILL`), 2 interrupt (`VINTR`), 3 quit
  (`VQUIT`), 4 suspend (`VSUSP`), 5 end of file (`VEOF`), 6 word erase
  (`VWERASE`), 7 literal next (`VLNEXT`), 8 start (`VSTART`), 9 stop
  (`VSTOP`), 10 reprint (`VREPRINT`), 11 discard (`VDISCARD`) — each the
  byte the user chose (`stty erase ^H`, `stty intr ^X`), or **-1** for
  one that is disabled (`stty intr undef`; the host's disabled value,
  measured black-box as 0 on linux and 255 on macOS, never reaches the
  program). Entries 6, 7, 10 and 11 are not POSIX's but both hosts have
  them; they act only with `EXTENDED` on. A line editor that turns
  `CANONICAL` and `SIGNALS` off reads these first so that erase, kill,
  interrupt and end of file keep the keys the user set. Nothing sets
  them (`stty` does); the list grows only at its end. A handle that is
  closed, forged or not a terminal is `io`; windows is `unsupported`.

- `[os.term.note]` **Design note: Ctrl-C without a handler** (s219).
  The issue (#622) asked for a meaning for `SIGINT`; a shell needs four
  things, and each was measured against dash 0.5.13.4 black-box through
  a pseudo-terminal: (1) to **survive** Ctrl-C at its prompt and while
  its child runs — a listen does it (the trampoline is a real handler),
  and an ignore does it too but would be inherited by every child;
  (2) to **learn** afterwards that one came — `os_signal_poll`, because
  dash at the prompt prints nothing at Ctrl-C (the terminal echoes
  `^C`) and answers only when the next line is read, so a poll after
  the read is the whole of it; (3) to give a child the **defaults** the
  shell does not keep for itself — `os_spawn_job`'s `defaults`, since
  dash's children start with nothing ignored although dash ignores
  `QUIT` and `TERMINATE`; (4) to **report** `128 + N` —
  `os_wait_status`. Job control adds the group, the foreground and its
  take-back, and line editing adds the mode. What stays out, by rule:
  no wolf code in a handler (`[os.signal.model]`) — a disposition is
  default, ignore or listen, nothing else; no `siginfo`; no
  `SA_RESTART` choice (a delivered signal never tears a read, so the
  prompt case is a poll after the read, not an `EINTR`; s234 adds the
  wait that ends for a key or a signal, `[os.signal.wait.fd]`); no stop
  reporting (`WUNTRACED`), no `os_kill` of a group, no `SIGCONT` — the
  next job-control lane (`fg`, `bg`, Ctrl-Z) owns them.
  **Ruled A (#57), 2026-10-10 (s219), each with its recommendation, which is what
  is implemented:**
  - **R1, the five meanings' names and bits.** (A) `INTERRUPT`,
    `SUSPEND`, `BG_READ`, `BG_WRITE`, `CHILD` at 16..256 — names of what
    happened, in the v1 table's style (`RELOAD`, not `HUP`); (B) the
    POSIX signal names (`INT`, `TSTP`, `TTIN`, `TTOU`, `CHLD`) — exact,
    but the table is by meaning on purpose; (C) a separate
    `os_signal_*_raw` family by number — rejected by
    `[os.signal.set]`. **Recommend A.**
  - **R2, the disposition calls.** (A) two calls,
    `os_signal_ignore(set)` and `os_signal_default(set)`, beside
    `os_signal_listen(set)`; (B) one `os_signal_disposition(set, how)`
    with an int `how` — one name, but an int that means a verb; (C) a
    flag on `os_signal_listen` — conflates hearing with surviving.
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R3, learning without waiting.** (A) `os_signal_poll(set) -> int`,
    0 for none; (B) `os_signal_wait` with a timeout argument — a new
    arity of an existing builtin, and a 0 timeout that means poll;
    (C) an `interrupted` row on the fs reads — every read site would
    have to handle it, and the trampoline does not tear reads.
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R4, the job spawn.** (A) `os_spawn_job(exe, args, map, group,
    tty, defaults)`, the descriptor map's sibling; (B) a builder value
    (a `Spawn` struct) — the builtin tier has no structs, std builds
    one over A; (C) separate `os_setpgid(h, g)` after the spawn — racy
    by construction (the child may exec and read before it lands).
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R5, a child's status.** (A) `os_wait_status(h) -> int`, the code or
    `-N`; (B) `128 + N` as the shell writes it — collides with a real
    exit code; (C) a `List[int]` pair (kind, number) — honest but
    clumsy for every caller. **Recommend A.**
  - **R6, the terminal calls.** (A) `os_pgid`, `os_term_foreground`,
    `os_term_set_foreground`, `os_term_mode`, `os_term_set_mode`, the
    mode one int as `[os.term.mode]` packs it; (B) the mode as four
    separate get/set calls — four round trips to save and restore;
    (C) a raw `termios` byte image — not portable between linux and
    macOS. **Recommend A.**
  - **R7, capabilities (with ruling #54's reasoning).** The
    dispositions, the poll, the job spawn, the pid and status and
    `os_term_set_foreground` are `exec` (process control); `os_pgid` is
    `env` (process context, as `os_cwd`); `os_term_foreground`,
    `os_term_mode` and `os_term_set_mode` are `io` (they act on a
    descriptor the program holds and start nothing, as `os_isatty`).
    **Recommend as listed.**
  - **R8, lupin's terminal half.** lupin forbids `unsafe` and links no
    libc, and stable Rust's std has `process_group` but no
    `tcsetpgrp`, `tcgetattr` or `sigaction`. (A) lupin mirrors what std
    reaches — `os_spawn_job` with a group and no `tty` or `defaults`,
    `os_proc_pid`, `os_wait_status` — and refuses the rest by name;
    (B) lupin takes a safe syscall crate (rustix) for the terminal and
    the group id, signals still refused. **Recommend A for this lane**;
    B is the maintainer's call.

- `[os.term.editor.note]` **Design note: what a line editor asks of the
  terminal** (s234; wolf-lang#719, W05; pelt's sh11 editor). An editor
  turns canonical input off and does the terminal's editing itself, so
  it needs four things `[os.term.mode]` did not give: the width to lay a
  line out in, word of a resize while a line is shown, a wait that a
  signal ends as well as a key, and the keys the user chose for erase,
  kill, interrupt and the rest — with flow control and the host's
  extended processing switchable, so Ctrl-S, Ctrl-Q, Ctrl-V and Ctrl-O
  reach it. Each was a witness in pelt (`notes/sh06-evidence/witness/`,
  `notes/sh11-evidence/witness/`). What stays out, by rule: no wolf code
  in a handler (`[os.signal.model]`); no restore of the mode when a
  program dies of a signal it cannot catch (the runtime restored nothing
  until s248, which restores a registered mode on every exit it owns,
  `[os.term.restore]`; a signal nobody listened for still runs no code);
  no setter for the special characters. **Ruled
  (s234; #73, 2026-10-13), each as its recommendation, which is what is
  implemented:**
  - **R1, the window's size.** (A) `os_term_size(fd) -> (int, int) !
    {io, unsupported}`, rows then columns, 0 for a size never told —
    `os_pipe`'s pair; (B) a `List[int]` of `winsize`'s four words, the
    pixel sizes included — two words nobody fills; (C) `os_term_rows`
    and `os_term_cols` — two calls a resize can fall between.
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R2, the resize.** No new surface: `RESIZE` is s232's (ruling #70
    R1, bit 16384, `SIGWINCH`), and a set with a bit outside the
    listenable meanings is already `io` on every set-taking call (#70
    R2). #719's "bit 512" predates s232; 512 is `USER`. **Recommend:
    record the reconciliation, change nothing.**
  - **R3, a wait a signal can end.** (A) `os_signal_wait_fd(fd, set) ->
    int ! {io, unsupported}`, the meaning or 0 when the descriptor is
    ready, nothing read, the meaning first; (B) `os_read_or_signal(fd,
    n, set) -> List[byte] ! {eof, io, signal}` (#719's first shape) —
    the read and the wait in one, but a row carries no payload, so a
    `signal` row still needs a poll to say which, and the read's own
    timing (`VTIME`) would apply to the wait as well; (C) `net_wait`'s
    shape over a descriptor list with the signal pipe as a member — puts
    the runtime's pipe in the program's hands, and `net_wait` takes net
    handles, not fs ones. A deadline argument was weighed and left out:
    the answer would need a third value, and on a terminal `VTIME`
    already times the read. **Recommend A.**
  - **R4, the special characters and the two flags.** (A)
    `os_term_chars(fd) -> List[int] ! {io, unsupported}`, twelve in a
    fixed order, -1 for disabled; `FLOW` (8, `IXON`) and `EXTENDED` (16,
    `IEXTEN`) in the mode int; (B) the characters as a `Map[str, int]` by
    name — a lookup per key, and a map where a fixed order serves;
    (C) the flags as a second int (`os_term_flags`) so the mode int keeps
    its old meaning — two values to save and restore, and every caller
    pays for the compatibility of hand-built modes. A hand-built mode
    without the two bits now turns `IXON` and `IEXTEN` off; the census
    of downstream callers is in the lane's evidence. **Recommend A.**
  - **R5, capabilities (with #57 R7's reasoning).** `os_term_size` and
    `os_term_chars` read a descriptor the program holds and start
    nothing: `io`, with `os_term_mode` (uncharged in a manifest, ruling
    #53). `os_signal_wait_fd` is signal control: `exec`, with
    `os_signal_wait`. **Recommend as listed.**
  - **R6, lupin.** lupin forbids `unsafe` and links no libc (#57 R8),
    and std has no `ioctl`, `tcgetattr` or `poll`. (A) it answers each
    call's shape rows (a refused set is `io`, a bad mode `invalid`, now
    with the two new bits valid) and refuses the three by name; (B) a
    safe syscall crate — the maintainer's call, as at #57 and #70.
    **Recommend A.**

- `[os.editor.calls.note]` **Design note: what the editor asks of the
  runtime** (s248; ruling #93; wolf-lang#794–#799, #802; yew
  `docs/MAP.md` §5–§6). yw00 mapped sagitta's 218 KLOC onto wolf and
  found what the port could not do; ruling #93 made R1 C (the runtime
  restores the terminal) and R2 A (one wait over descriptors and
  signals with a deadline). s248 adds `os_term_restore_at_exit`
  (`[os.term.restore]`), `os_signal_wait_fds` (`[os.signal.wait.fds]`),
  `fs_sync` and `fs_sync_dir` (`[os.fs.sync]`), `fs_realpath`
  (`[os.fs.realpath]`), `os_clock_ns` (`[os.clock.ns]`), the mode's bits
  5..7 (`[os.term.mode]`), and `wolf test`'s discovery of each test
  file's own `test_*` (wolf-lang#799; `wolf test`'s own module doc,
  `crates/wolf_driver/src/test_cmd.rs`; no clause here). **Rulings asked** (each with the lane's
  recommendation, which is what is implemented):
  - **R1, the restore's rows (#794).** (A) `{invalid, io, unsupported}`:
    a handle that is closed, forged or not a terminal is `io`, as for
    every `[os.term]` call, and so is a duplicate the host will not make;
    (B) the contract's `{invalid, unsupported}`, with those handles
    `invalid` — a word the family keeps for a mode's shape. **Recommend
    A.**
  - **R2, the wait's answer (#795).** When a meaning and a descriptor are
    both ready: (A) `(-1, m)`, the meaning alone, as `os_signal_wait_fd`
    answers it — the descriptor stays ready and answers the next wait;
    (B) `(i, m)`, both — one answer more, and every caller handles a
    pair that is two events. Among ready descriptors the LOWEST index.
    The set takes the one shape rule (`io` for an empty set: a wait on
    descriptors alone passes a set it listens for). **Recommend A.**
  - **R3, the exclusive create (#796).** (A) No third spelling: open
    mode 4 and `fs_open_perm(path, 4, perm)` are the exclusive create on
    every machine, `exists` for a taken name, measured at 0.2.33 (lupin
    too); `[os.fs.sync]` names them in the save; (B) `fs_create_new(path,
    perm)`, the contract's name, a third spelling of `fs_open_perm(path,
    4, perm)` for every implementation and std to carry. **Recommend
    A.**
  - **R4, the directory's sync on windows (#796).** (A) `unsupported` by
    name: no directory is opened as a file there; (B) answer ok and do
    nothing, NTFS ordering the rename itself — a call that says it synced
    and did not. `invalid` for a name that is not a directory.
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R5, capabilities (with #57 R7's and #73 R5's reasoning).**
    `os_term_restore_at_exit` is `io` (a descriptor the program holds,
    nothing started, with `os_term_set_mode`); `os_signal_wait_fds` is
    `exec` (signal control, with `os_signal_wait_fd`); the syncs and
    `fs_realpath` are `fs`; `os_clock_ns` is the Clock (refused at
    comptime, uncharged in a manifest, with `time_now_ms`). **Recommend
    as listed.**
  - **R6, `wolf test`'s discovery (#799).** (A) each test file's OWN
    `test_*` — the entry of the package built for it, what `wolf test`'s
    module doc has said since s39 ("inside a test file"); (B) every file
    of that package, the contract's words — a `test_*` helper in a plain
    file of the directory would run once for every test file beside it,
    as each one's test. **Recommend A.**
  - **R7, the raw-mode bits (#802).** (A) three bits whose 0 is the usual
    setting — `RAW_CR` (32, `ICRNL` cleared), `RAW_OUTPUT` (64, `OPOST`
    cleared), `STRIP8` (128, `ISTRIP` set): every mode int a released
    program or std reads or builds on a usual terminal is unchanged;
    (B) #802's `CR_NL`, `OUTPUT_POST`, `STRIP8` as flags that are set
    when on — `os_term_mode` on a usual terminal would answer 96 more
    than at 0.2.33, and wolf-std's released `pack` drops bits 5..7, so
    its restore of a saved mode would turn `OPOST` off and leave the
    shell after every `std.term` program writing LF without CR; (C) one
    editor-raw flag clearing `cfmakeraw`'s set — not reversible through
    one int (the runtime could not restore what it cleared without
    hidden state). **Recommend A.**
  - **R8, the checked machine's restore (#794; the contract: "restore on
    its own exit path, or refuse by name: propose").** (A) it restores on
    its own end, every verdict — `conform-run --checked` leaves a terminal
    as a compiled program does; (B) it refuses the call by name — a
    checked run of an editor would refuse at its first line. **Recommend
    A.**
  lupin 0.1.54 and 0.1.55 resolve none of the six names, and the mode's
  bits 5..7 are `invalid` there. From 0.1.56, all six resolve (is79,
  wolf-interp#268): the restore and wait answer their shape rows, then
  refuse by name; `fs_sync` and `fs_sync_dir` use `File::sync_all`,
  `fs_realpath` uses `fs::canonicalize` inside the served tree, and
  `os_clock_ns` uses `Instant`. The mode bits are fields. A wait fixture
  that advances past the newly resolved wait can now stop at its listen,
  which remains a by-name refusal, not a failure to resolve the wait.

## §9 The json query tier `[os.json]`

(Written 2026-10-10, s224 — wolf-lang#124, ruling B22 of 2026-09-11.)

- `[os.json.dup]` **A repeated object name is last-wins.** RFC 8259 §4
  says an object's names SHOULD be unique and leaves a repeat to the
  implementation; the json builtins (`json_get`, `json_type`,
  `json_len`, and the path segments they walk) read an object as ONE
  member per name, at the position where that name first appears,
  holding the value of its LAST occurrence — a `Map` assignment, as
  `std.json.parse` reads the same text and as JavaScript, Python and
  serde (with preserved order) do. So `json_get("{\"a\": 1, \"a\": 2}",
  "a")` is `2` and `json_len` of that object is `1`; a path walks
  through the last container a repeated name holds; a nested object
  that `json_get` re-renders compactly carries the name once, in its
  first position, with its last value (`{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}` renders
  `{"a":3,"b":2}`). The ROOT container's `json_get` is unchanged: it
  answers the document's own text, trimmed, repeats and all, because
  that answer is the source, not a rendering. `json_valid` accepts a
  repeat, as RFC 8259 does. Every machine answers alike: the checked
  machine (`wolf_mem::json`), native and release (`wolf_rt::json`,
  pinned to the first by `json_parity`), and lupin. Before s224 all
  four read the FIRST occurrence and counted every one. **The cost,
  stated:** none a program can see — the parser keeps one member per
  name as it reads (a scan for a small object, a name index past 16
  members), and every query already parsed the whole text. Witnesses:
  `corpus/json/dup_*.lu` (seven rows) and
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/json_dup_lanes.rs`, on four machines.

---

## §10 The clock `[os.clock.ns]`

(Written 2026-10-19, s248 — wolf-lang#798; yew's G8, ruling #93.)

- `[os.clock.ns]` **The monotonic clock at nanoseconds.**
  **`os_clock_ns() -> int`** answers the nanoseconds since an arbitrary
  process-local anchor on the host's finest monotonic clock — the clock
  `time_now_ms` reads, from **the same anchor** (`[os.host.sigs]`'s time
  tier): `os_clock_ns() / 1000000` read after a `time_now_ms()` is never
  smaller than it. A value is a duration to compare and subtract, never
  a timestamp; it never goes backwards and never fails (no row), and it
  saturates at the largest int, 292 years from the anchor. The host's
  clock is `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` on linux, the mach clock on
  macOS and `QueryPerformanceCounter`
  on windows, as Rust's `Instant` reads each; the checked machine reads
  the same host clock from its own anchor. **Why** (yew `docs/MAP.md`
  G8): an editor's latency gates are nanoseconds (a keypress to its
  paint, p99 at most 5 ms), and the finest clock a program had was
  milliseconds — twenty rounds of about 100 us of work, timed by
  `time_now_ms`, read 0 in 19 or 20 of them (yw00's witness, at 0.2.32
  and 0.2.33). It is the clock: Clock at comptime, refused there with the
  ms tier, and charged nothing in a manifest (`[os.host.sigs]`).
  **The cost, stated:** one host clock read, as `time_now_ms`. lupin
  0.1.54 and 0.1.55 do not resolve it (wolf-interp#268). From 0.1.56,
  lupin reads its monotonic `Instant` anchor at nanosecond precision,
  with the same saturation (is79). Witness:
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/editor_calls_lanes.rs`
  (`fixtures/editor_calls/clock_ns.lu`): the twenty rounds, none 0, on
  every machine (the binaries also under `taskset -c 0-3` on linux).

---

## §11 The host `[os.uname]`

(Written 2026-10-21, s253 — wolf-lang#819; yew's G31.)

- `[os.uname]` **Which OS and which architecture the program runs
  on.** **`os_name() -> str`** and **`os_arch() -> str`**, no row
  (ruling asked, `[os.process.calls.note]` R5, the recommendation
  implemented). The words are fixed. On a unix host they are what the
  KERNEL answers (`uname(2)`), not what the program was built for:
  `os_name` is its `sysname` in lowercase, Darwin's as **`macos`** —
  **`linux`**, **`macos`**, **`freebsd`**, and **`pax`** on PAX, whose
  kernel answers `PAX` (a static linux binary run there names its kernel;
  the px lane to confirm); `os_arch` is its `machine` in lowercase, with
  macOS's and the BSDs' spellings of the two tier-1 architectures as
  linux's — **`x86_64`** (`amd64`) and **`aarch64`** (`arm64`). A process
  under emulation answers what its kernel tells it. Windows has no
  `uname`: **`windows`**, and the architecture the program was built for.
  A kernel outside these answers its own `sysname` and `machine`,
  lowercased: the vocabulary is fixed for every host wolf builds for, and
  says of any other what that kernel calls itself. Read once a process
  (a kernel's name does not change while the process runs). **Why** (yew
  `docs/MAP.md` G31): a program chooses a clipboard backend, a path
  convention or a signal number by its host — sagitta chooses pbcopy at
  compile time on macOS on arm64 — and the port could only look at
  `PATH` (`os_name` met E0301 at 0.2.33, yew's `witness/host-os`).
  Measured (s253): `linux` and `x86_64` on kasumi and CI's linux runner,
  `macos` and `aarch64` on CI's macOS runner, `windows` and `x86_64` on
  CI's windows runner, every machine the same as the test's own `uname`.
  Charged `env` (with `os_cpus`) and refused at comptime (the host that
  compiles is not the one that runs). **The checked machine** answers the
  host's (the `wolf` process's own `uname`). **lupin 0.1.55** does not
  resolve either name; its mirror answers its own host's. **The cost,
  stated:** one `uname` a process. Witness:
  `crates/wolf_driver/tests/process_calls_lanes.rs`
  (`fixtures/process_calls/host.lu`), on every machine.

- `[os.process.calls.note]` **Design note: the process calls' rulings
  asked** (s253; wolf-lang#811, #812, #815, #819). Each recommendation
  is what is built.
  - **R1, the core calls' shape (#811).** (A) three calls: the reader
    `os_core_limit()`, the setter `os_set_core_limit(soft, hard)`, and
    `os_core_off()` for "no core, ever" (`[os.proc.core]`); (B) the one
    setter of the contract's sketch, `os_core_limit(soft, hard)`, which
    at a soft of 0 would also make the process undumpable on linux, and
    no reader. B ties the attribute's other effects (no `ptrace` attach,
    `/proc` files the super-user's) to a limit a program sets for its
    children too, and leaves "the limit I was born with" (pax's sigwolf)
    unreadable. **Recommend A.**
  - **R2, `os_core_off` off linux.** (A) the soft limit 0, where a core is
    a file the limit governs (macOS, the BSDs); (B) `unsupported` there.
    **Recommend A.**
  - **R3, the C library's numbers (#812, `[os.signal.host.reserved]`).**
    (A) `invalid`, by name, in `os_signal_ignore_one`,
    `os_signal_default_one` and `os_exit_signal`, on every machine and
    every C library, before the host is asked; the sends and the words
    unchanged; (B) `io` kept for the two disposition calls (their
    released row) and `invalid` for `os_exit_signal` (it has no `io`
    row); (C) release them: `os_exit_signal` ends the process by one
    through the raw `rt_sigaction`, past glibc's wrapper. A is one row for
    one reason; its cost is the two disposition calls' row for 32 and 33
    moving from `io` to `invalid` (boreutils' `timeout`, the one caller
    in the org, swallows the row). **Recommend A.**
  - **R4, the adoption's shape (#815, `[os.proc.adopt]`).** (A)
    `fs_adopt(fd) -> int ! {invalid, io, unsupported}`: the handle owns
    and closes the descriptor, close-on-exec on adoption, the rule "open
    and not close-on-exec"; (B) a duplicate, the inherited number left
    open and unowned — in every child the program starts, and two numbers
    for one file. **Recommend A.**
  - **R5, the host query's shape (#819, `[os.uname]`).** (A) two calls,
    `os_name() -> str` and `os_arch() -> str`, no row (`os_name` is the
    name yew reached for; the words are Rust's `std::env::consts`
    vocabulary), the words the kernel's at run time; (B) the contract's
    `os_host() -> (str, str)`, a pair of strings no builtin answers yet,
    a new shape on every machine and in lupin; (C) the build's words at
    compile time, which cannot see PAX. **Recommend A.**
  - **R6, capabilities.** The reads (`os_name`, `os_arch`,
    `os_core_limit`) `env`, with `os_cpus`; the set and the off call
    `exec`, with `os_exit_signal`; the adoption `fs`, with the family.
    All six refused at comptime. **Recommend as listed.**
  - **R7, the checked machine.** It answers the host's words, reads and
    sets the `wolf` process's own limit and attribute, and adopts its
    inherited descriptors: the process the program runs as, as for the
    dispositions. **Recommend as listed.**
